excerpt_i18n.en: Nvidia is once again at the center of attention. Within just a few days, two seemingly unrelated events have dominated headlines: a live discussion between Stanford professor Fei-Fei Li and Nvidia's chief scientist Jim Fan on the topic "Teaching AI to Act in the World," and the first public appearance of Madison Huang, daughter of Jensen Huang and senior director of product marketing at Nvidia, in a dialogue with Xie Chen, founder of Lightwheel, exploring simulation, embodied intelligence, and the future of Sim2Real. One event represents the academic sphere, while the other symbolizes the future leadership of the industry. When viewed together, they reveal a common narrative: Nvidia is aggressively advancing its simulation computing strategy. Jensen Huang has set this direction for the next decade, using three pillars—Omniverse, Isaac Sim, and Physical AI—to build an "intelligent physical world computing network" that bridges the virtual and real worlds. In essence, Nvidia aims not just to develop more powerful computing capabilities but to create a system that enables AI to "learn and act in the world," allowing machines to not only understand data but truly grasp the world itself. Nvidia is playing a long game. A new landscape of three "computers" has emerged. Over the past decade, Nvidia has quietly transformed from a graphics card manufacturer into an AI-focused company.

Un evento representaba el ámbito académico, mientras el otro el industrial.
